interJudgeAgreement.definition: A second model re-judged a prefix of the same drawn sample, blind to the first model's verdict, with the identical prompt. Kappa is on the three-way verdict; brokenAgreement is on the binary broken / not-broken call the filter actually uses.

sampling.unit: headword link (one sentence paired with one canon headword it was selected for)
sampling.design: Stratified random sample. Strata are HSK band group of the headword (1-3 / 4-6 / 7) crossed with headword character length (1 / 2 / 3+) — the two axes the known defects cluster on. Allocation is a floor of 40 per stratum plus the remainder proportional to stratum population, so every stratum is individually reportable and the corpus-wide estimate is still carried by the large strata. Corpus-wide rates are population-weighted with a finite-population correction; a simple mean over the sample would over-weight the deliberately over-sampled small strata.

results.definition: broken = the judge says the sentence is ungrammatical, incoherent, or misuses the headword. awkward = parseable but stilted or unidiomatic. good = natural Mandarin. `notClean` is broken + awkward.

filter.note: Computable predictors of brokenness, each scored against the judged labels above, and the filter policies built from them. Every rate is weighted by stratum population; the raw sample over-samples the small strata on purpose. Nothing here modifies data/sentences.jsonl.

predictors.hypothesis: A one-character headword is often a bound morpheme, a polyphone, or a fragment of the word that carries the meaning. The generator has to build a whole sentence around it and has the least to work with.
Band 7 is the merged 7-9 range: 5,636 of the canon's 11,092 words, the advanced and low-frequency tail. The hand read of 42 sentences put the defects here.
If the headword does not survive segmentation as its own token it is buried inside a longer word — 生 inside 医生 — and the sentence teaches the longer word, not this one.
A common noun immediately followed by a title, or preceded by 姓 or 叫, has been pressed into service as a surname. This is the 室先生 failure.
CC-CEDICT says the headword is an abbreviation, a variant, or a bound form.
CC-CEDICT lists the headword as a surname, so the generator had a licence to misuse it.
A sentence in the bottom decile of length for its own grade band is likely a frame with the headword dropped in rather than a sentence about anything. 这次难很大 is six characters.
Eight characters or fewer leaves no room for the context that makes a use natural.
An `easy` link is a sentence graded below its headword's own band — the headword is the hardest thing in it and everything else is trivial, which is the shape of a forced frame.
A `stretch` link carries material above the headword's band and has more room to go wrong.
A token outside HSK 3.0 altogether may be a typo, a name, or a word the source invented.
A headword with little or no corpus attestation is one the source had few real examples of.
A ZSG-7 sentence contains advanced material anywhere in it, not just in the headword.

policies.description: Drop only the three highest-precision signals: the headword used as a name, an `easy` link, and a headword that does not survive segmentation. No coverage protection — included to price what the coverage protection is worth.
`surgical`, but never strip a headword's last sentence.

`surgical-keep-last` plus every single-character headword link. The recommended policy: it removes the two things the labels actually convict — a headword used wrongly, and a headword too short to build a sentence around — and nothing else.
`balanced` plus sentences in the bottom sixth of length for their own band.
`strict` plus every sentence of eight characters or fewer.
Drop every single-character-headword link with no coverage protection. Included to price the coverage protection on the predictor that does the most work.
Ship bands 1-6 and drop band 7 entirely. The simple option the brief asked to be evaluated. Coverage protection is meaningless here: the point is to remove headwords.
`bands-1-6` plus the surgical drops on what remains.

heldOut.method: Labels split by alternating within each stratum, so both halves keep the sampling design. The individual predictors are a priori and are scored on all labels; the union that makes up the recommended policy was chosen by looking at those scores, so it is re-scored here on a half it was not chosen on.

recommendation.summary: Apply "balanced": drop the 3708 links (11.16%) it selects, never strip a headword's last sentence, and ship the disclosure below anyway. Broken falls from 12.85% to 8.51% and headword coverage does not move: 99.82%, the same 11072 of 11092 canon rows the corpus covers today.
rationale: The rate is worse than the 42-sentence read suggested. Measured: 12.85% broken (95% CI 10.08%-15.63%) against an eyeball estimate of 8-10%, plus a further 12.11% awkward-but-parseable. And 12.85% is a floor, not a point: on the six hand-found defects the judge grades 4 of them "awkward" rather than "broken", so it under-calls severity in the direction that flatters the corpus.

The failure axis is headword LENGTH, not band. Single-character headwords are 42.78% broken against a 12.85% base rate — 42.31% at band 1-3, 50.00% at band 4-6, 35.29% at band 7, so the effect holds at every level. Band 7 itself is 10.70% broken, which is BELOW the base rate: it is anti-predictive. The prior that band 7 is the problem does not survive contact with the labels, and it survived this long because band 7 is half the corpus, so half the defects are in it by arithmetic.

Keeping each headword's last sentence is what makes the filter affordable. The same single-character drop costs 14.81% of headword coverage without that rule and nothing with it, for a residual the sample cannot tell apart — 7.71% against 8.51%, on intervals that overlap almost entirely. A weak sentence for a word is still better evidence the word exists than no sentence at all, and coverage is the corpus's headline claim.

Stopping here is a judgement about the marginal rule, not about the direction. "strict" adds sentence-short-for-band and reaches 7.17%, but the links it adds over "balanced" are only 7/33 broken (0.21, 95% CI 10.68%-37.75%) against a sample base rate near 0.17 — indistinguishable from dropping at random. It costs another 3003 links, and 6345 headwords keep a full three-sentence triad under it against 9064 under "balanced". Not worth it on this evidence; re-run with more labels if you want to revisit it.

This is an improvement, not a fix. The residual interval [5.61%, 11.40%] is nowhere near zero: roughly one sentence in twelve is still defective after the filter, and the judge under-calls severity. Whatever ships, the disclosure ships with it — a measured and published defect rate is a far better position than a filtered corpus that implies there is nothing left to declare.

rejected.because: The worst option on the board, on every axis at once. Drops 50.77% of links, takes headword coverage from 99.82% to 49.13% — 5,642 canon words lose every sentence they have — and the residual broken rate GOES UP, to 15.07%. Band 7 is where the two-character headwords live; cutting it concentrates the single-character ones that are the actual defect.
Lands at 7.71% residual, which this sample cannot distinguish from "balanced" at 8.51%, while destroying 14.81% of headword coverage. Pure cost.
Drops 30.09% of the corpus to land at 7.46%, which is WORSE than "strict" at 7.17%. Past a point the length rules stop selecting for defects and start selecting for short sentences.

The fallback if dropping 11.16% of links is judged too expensive: 4.63% dropped at precision 0.66 — the highest of any policy — for a residual of 10.03%. Two fifths of the benefit for a quarter of the cut, and it leaves 9956 headwords with a full triad.
